title: Musk Vows Affordable Starlink in India, Escalating Feud With Ambani Before Jio's Record IPO
excerpt: In X posts, Elon Musk promised affordable satellite internet to take on Reliance Jio, saying competition would benefit ordinary Indians — days before Jio Platforms' record $106 billion IPO.
body:
• Elon Musk said SpaceX will price Starlink's satellite internet "affordably" in India to take on Mukesh Ambani's low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio Platforms' record IPO.
  • Musk wrote on X that competition would "greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices," adding that Ambani's profits would be lower but he "is not going out of business."
  • Jio Platforms is targeting a valuation of about $106 billion in what would be India's largest-ever IPO; both Starlink and Jio's own satellite venture are awaiting final security clearance to launch.
  • For Indian consumers: a price war between Starlink and Jio in satellite broadband could bring cheaper rural connectivity, but neither service has a launch date yet.

Elon Musk said he would price Starlink's satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani's low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio's parent launches India's largest-ever IPO, Reuters reported from Bengaluru on Saturday.

Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of about $106 billion in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink, Jio's own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch in India.

"Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable. The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does."

— Elon Musk, on X

Context: a feud that keeps escalating

The billionaire's remarks were the latest in a series of posts on his social media platform X in which he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and Ambani of stalling Starlink's entry into one of the world's biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio. The posts mark a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi.

India's government has denied any bias in the approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch — including Starlink's and Jio's — are all awaiting final security clearance. The dispute has drawn in politicians and commentators across India, with some framing it as a sovereignty and security question and others as straightforward competition policy.

Why affordability is the whole game

Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about 8 cents per gigabyte — among the lowest in the world. Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio into India's dominant carrier, and it is the same playbook Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle incumbent telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the United States.

The economics of satellite broadband, however, are brutally different from terrestrial networks. Starlink's hardware and monthly fees are an order of magnitude above Indian mobile plans. Musk's promise implies either heavy subsidisation or a stripped-down India tier — neither of which SpaceX has detailed.

Impact and analysis

The timing is not accidental. With Jio's mega-IPO days away, Musk is doing what he does best: injecting himself into a rival's defining moment. But the substance matters more than the theatre. Satellite broadband is India's best near-term hope for connecting its hardest-to-reach villages, where fibre will never go. A genuine Starlink–Jio price war could accelerate rural connectivity by years.

The risk is that the feud itself becomes the story and the clearance process gets more politicised, not less. Both ventures need the same security sign-off; neither has it. Until that changes, the affordable-Starlink promise is marketing against a launch date that does not exist.

Diaspora angle

For NRIs with family in rural India, satellite broadband is the technology most likely to change what a video call home looks like. A competitive satellite market could mean relatives in areas where even 4G is patchy finally getting reliable high-speed access — and Jio's IPO gives global investors, including diaspora portfolios, direct exposure to the outcome.

What's next

Watch three things: the Jio Platforms IPO pricing and listing pop, the security-clearance decisions for the satellite ventures, and whether Musk attaches a number to "affordable." Without a price and a launch date, this week's vow is a shot across Ambani's bow — fired from orbit.
